clue.text: Before working hours, find time to make time

indicators.note: the shuffled letters stand before the piece for working, which follows them
the words hours and find time are used as raw material to make something new, so they are rearranged

parts.note: a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: Advice to squeeze some extra time out of the day before work starts.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'time' is part of the fodder and the second is the definition: the clue says time twice for two different jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Physicists call time the dimension that follows length, breadth and depth, the one after the three spatial ones.

clue.text: Health one exchanged for a state of corpulence

indicators.note: one letter is swapped out and the next one put in its place

parts.note: physical fitness is good health
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Trading in good health for being overweight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanged for' swaps the I (one) in FITNESS for A, giving FATNESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Corpulence is being fat, so a state of corpulence is the condition of being fat.

clue.text: Say it's complete

definitions.meaning: to say something is to speak or voice it
as an adjective, total or absolute

explanation.definitionFit: Utter is both a verb meaning to speak and an adjective meaning total or out-and-out.

clue.text: I'm off to old resort on northbound tube

indicators.note: to re-sort the words to old is to put their letters in a new order
in a down clue, going north means reading the word upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: a pipe is a tube

explanation.surface: Someone saying goodbye as they head off to an old seaside town by London Underground going north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday town but is read as re-sort, rearranging TO OLD into TOODLE; 'northbound' turns PIPE upwards into PIP. The 'tube' looks like the Underground.
explanation.definitionFit: Toodle-pip is old-fashioned British slang for goodbye, what you say as you leave.

clue.text: It captures the wee bairn's first steps

indicators.note: the first letter of the word bairn's is taken

parts.note: a ladder is a set of steps

explanation.surface: A Scottish toddler taking their first little steps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wee' looks like the Scots word for small next to bairn (a Scottish child), but in the definition it means urine. B is the first letter of bairn's.
explanation.definitionFit: The bladder is the organ that collects and holds urine, so it captures the wee.

clue.text: Homeless individual willing to occupy recess

indicators.note: one piece takes up residence inside the other, sitting within it

parts.note: a bay is a recess in a wall or room
glad, as in glad to help, means willing

explanation.surface: A homeless person happy to shelter in an alcove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recess' suggests a break from work, but here it is an alcove in a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A bag lady is a homeless woman who carries her belongings in bags.

clue.text: A party given to cause embarrassment

parts.note: a bash is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: Throwing a party in order to embarrass someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash is to make someone feel ashamed or embarrassed.

clue.text: See 1 across
Publish that Scottish-American author

parts.note: newspapers run a story when they publish it
yon is Scots for that, as in yon hill

explanation.surface: An instruction to bring out a book by a Scottish-American writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scottish-American' reads as one word, but 'Scottish' turns 'that' into YON, leaving 'American author' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Damon Runyon was an American writer known for his stories of Broadway gamblers and gangsters.

clue.text: Grinding device one's affected?

definitions.meaning: a machine that grinds meat into small pieces
someone who minces, walking or speaking in an affected, dainty manner

explanation.definitionFit: A mincer chops meat finely, and to mince also means to walk with exaggerated delicacy.

clue.text: Personally, colourful work rubbish — go into weaving

parts.note: tat is cheap, tasteless rubbish

indicators.note: weaving interlaces strands, so the letters of go into are woven into a new order

explanation.surface: A complaint that a bright piece of art is junk and should be woven into something better.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic paraphrase: colourful work done on one's own person.
explanation.definitionFit: Tattooing puts colourful designs on a person's own skin, artwork done on the body itself.

clue.text: Bill has little time for paperwork

parts.note: a bill is a poster or advertisement, an ad
min is short for minute, a small amount of time

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill too busy for the office forms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a name; it is an advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: Admin, short for administration, is routine office work such as forms and filing.

clue.text: Corporate fraudsters not entirely left to sign on!

indicators.note: the company name loses its last letter, so it is not there in full

parts.note: Enron was the US energy company that collapsed in 2001 after accounting fraud

explanation.surface: A remark that crooked bosses who are not wholly gone still have to sign on for benefits.
explanation.walkthrough: Enron was the US energy company whose 2001 collapse exposed huge accounting fraud.
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol is to sign up or register, as on a course.

clue.text: To make an impact with religion, first bend over

indicators.note: the turned piece comes first, ahead of the religion
over means turned over, so the word for bend is read backwards

parts.note: an arc is a bend or curve
Shinto is the native religion of Japan

explanation.surface: Advice to make a mark on faith by first bowing down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bend over' reads as a bow but is ARC turned round; Shinto is the native religion of Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: To crash into something is to collide with it, striking it hard.

clue.text: Goalkeeper's bung

definitions.meaning: a plug or cork that closes a bottle or hole

explanation.definitionFit: A stopper is a cork or plug, and a goalkeeper is sometimes called a shot-stopper.

clue.text: Company chairman is calling for rescue?

definitions.text: Company chairman is calling for rescue?

parts.words: Company chairman is calling for rescue?
parts.note: a chairman sits above the company board, and the cry man ... is what someone shouts when a person falls off a ship and needs rescuing

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'chairman is' as 'chair-man is': the man has gone off the boat, and he is also the one over the board of the company.
explanation.definitionFit: Over the board is where a chairman sits, and man overboard is the shout for a sailor needing rescue.

clue.text: You Nazis provoke endlessly, asking for word of compliance

parts.note: ye is the old form of you
the SS was the Nazi paramilitary force

indicators.note: the word for provoke loses its final letter

parts.note: to ire is to anger or provoke

explanation.surface: A warning not to goad Nazis endlessly when they ask for obedience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts IRE (provoke) to IR. 'asking for' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Yes sir is the respectful phrase used to agree to an order.

clue.text: Second double entendre, perhaps, suggests going for a slash?

parts.note: a double entendre is one example of playing with words

explanation.surface: A rude double meaning implying a trip to the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going for a slash' is British slang for urinating; here it is slashing with a blade.
explanation.definitionFit: Swordplay is fencing, where combatants slash at one another with blades.

clue.text: Rash head of state going after political leader in the Guardian?

indicators.note: the first letter of state comes after the rest
the leading letter sits inside the word for the paper

parts.note: in the Guardian newspaper is here, in these very pages

indicators.note: the leader of political is its first letter
the head of the word state is its first letter

explanation.surface: A hasty newspaper story about a head of state chasing a party leader.
explanation.walkthrough: P (political leader) goes inside HERE (the Guardian, where the clue is printed), then S (head of state) comes after.
explanation.definitionFit: Herpes is a viral infection that shows itself as a rash of blisters.

clue.text: Bit of light paper superior to wood

indicators.note: in a down clue, superior means placed above, so this piece sits on top

parts.note: the Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a beam is a length of timber

explanation.surface: A claim that paper is better than wood.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunbeam is a ray, a narrow shaft of sunlight.

clue.text: Sunk, having inhaled last of air?

definitions.text: Sunk, having inhaled last of air?

indicators.note: breathing in takes something inside, so a letter goes into the word

parts.note: to sink a drink is to down it

indicators.note: last of means only the closing letter of the word air is used, the bit left at its end

explanation.surface: Someone going under after breathing in the last of their air.
explanation.walkthrough: R (last of air) goes into DOWNED (sunk, as a drink); the whole clue also describes drowning.
explanation.definitionFit: Drowned means died under water, sunk after taking in water instead of air.

clue.text: European nations cutting scandal, becoming honest

indicators.note: one piece cuts into the middle of the other

parts.note: dirt is scandalous gossip
EC is the European Community, a group of European nations

explanation.surface: European countries cleaning up a scandal and turning honest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' puts EC into DIRT.
explanation.definitionFit: Direct means straightforward and frank, honest in speech.

clue.text: Muslim possessing nothing quite like fuel?

definitions.meaning: a member of a Muslim religious order living in poverty
derv is diesel fuel, and -ish means somewhat like

explanation.definitionFit: Dervishes are Sufi ascetics who take vows of poverty, and the word splits into derv plus -ish.

clue.text: If not without cakes, perhaps, remove topping

indicators.note: the first letter is taken off the top of the word

parts.note: buns are cakes, so having none is being bunless

explanation.surface: A suggestion to scrape the icing off if you have no cakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remove topping' drops the B of BUNLESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Unless means except if, that is, if not.

clue.text: Head back, returning around home, which is easy

parts.note: nob is slang for the head

indicators.note: the reversed piece goes around the word for home
the word for back is read in reverse

parts.note: the rear is the back
in means at home

explanation.surface: Turning back around towards home is easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which is easy' stands for a thing that is easy, the sense the noun answer carries.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-brainer is a decision so simple it needs no thought.

clue.text: Field entered by sportsmen, ultimately?

indicators.note: the last letter goes into the word for field

parts.note: an area is a field or zone

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of sportsmen

explanation.surface: The ground that athletes finally walk out onto.
explanation.walkthrough: N (last of sportsmen) goes into AREA; the whole clue also describes a sports venue.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a stadium, an enclosed ground where sportsmen compete.

clue.text: Company in English city dropping by to offer interior design

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the shortened city
the city loses the letters given by the word that follows

parts.note: Derby is a city in the English Midlands

explanation.surface: A firm in a Midlands town skipping a visit to provide room design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping by' looks like paying a visit; it takes the letters BY out of DERBY, a city in the English Midlands, leaving DER.
explanation.definitionFit: Decor is the style of furnishing and decoration of a room.

clue.text: Brew some magic up, Pasquale!

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An exclamation urging Pasquale to conjure up a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea, a brew.

clue.text: Lift has yet to arrive, stuck on ninth in skyscraper

indicators.note: the late piece is attached after the single letter
count to the ninth letter of skyscraper

parts.note: something that has yet to arrive is late

explanation.surface: Complaint that the elevator is late, stuck on the ninth floor of a tower block.
explanation.walkthrough: The ninth letter of skyscraper is E; LATE is stuck on after it. 'Lift' looks like an elevator but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To elate someone is to lift their spirits.

clue.text: Trees from English city arranged with Paul

indicators.note: the letters are put in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Woodland in an English city planted with the setter's help.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul is the name of this puzzle's setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Eucalypti is a plural of eucalyptus, the Australian gum tree.

clue.text: Admires spinning sort of throw

indicators.note: spinning sends the letters of admires whirling into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone admiring a throw with plenty of spin.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidearm throw is a baseball delivery with the arm swung sideways, below the shoulder.

clue.text: Minor route with variable parking in English city

indicators.note: the two letters go inside the city

parts.note: Bath is a city in the west of England
Y is a letter used for an algebraic variable

explanation.surface: A side road with changeable parking in a West Country city.
explanation.walkthrough: Y (variable) and P (parking) go inside BATH, a city in the west of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A bypath is a side path or byway, a lesser route.
